articles.title: Beware ‘sun, sea and surgery’ cosmetic tourism packages, experts advise
articles.summary: British College of Aesthetic Medicine launches checklist as part of ‘vet it before you get it’ campaign. Cosmetic tourism is often sold as a package of sun, sea and surgery, but experts have said travelling overseas for procedures can end in infections, disfigurement and death.
body: Nora Nugent, a consultant plastic surgeon and former president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, said travelling to countries such as Turkey for surgery came with myriad risks – and not just on the operating table.

“Actually, the risks start from the moment you step on the plane to after you return home, and until you’re fully healed and you’re out of the clotting risk time,” she said, noting that travel itself could increase the risks of clots. A lack of in-person aftercare is also a concern.

The British College of Aesthetic Medicine has launched a checklist as part of its “vet it before you get it” campaign, intended to help potential patients make better and safer choices about overseas cosmetic surgery.

As well as setting out red flags to look out for, the campaign suggests those seeking cosmetic surgery independently verify a surgeon’s qualifications, determine what emergency facilities are available near the chosen clinic and find out what insurance the practitioner has in place.

articles.title: Charity shops have value in the community | Letter
articles.summary: They help volunteers to develop skills, make friends and find employment, says Antony David Davies. Your article on the declining profitability of charity shops struck a chord with me ( UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market, 31 October ).
body: Charity shops were never just about making money. They provided affordable goods for people who needed them and, equally importantly, opportunities to gain confidence, develop skills, make friends and sometimes find their way back into employment. For some, volunteering is their first step back into society after a difficult period in their lives.

Of course, charity shops must pay their way. I spent six years managing a Salvation Army shop, substantially increasing its turnover, only to see it eventually close. So I understand the financial realities only too well. But I wonder whether in the pursuit of profitability and increasingly professional retail operations, parts of the sector have lost sight of their original purpose.

articles.summary: I love jeans but struggled to style trends without feeling like a teen. Experts recommended options from Spanx, Frame, Levi’s and more. The 12 makeup and 13 skincare products I swear by. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things. I love jeans.
body: I love jeans. And I love following the newest trends. But as a woman of a certain age, I have struggled with how to show off the latest silhouettes without feeling like I’m chasing my youth. When baggy jeans came back into fashion, I was thrilled! But as I tried to style them on myself, the tees and sneakers I paired them with made me feel a little bit like a teen. My foray into baggy jeans moved me to further investigation – I decided to find out about all the new styles being worn here and now, and how to help me (and others!) wear them best.

The denim landscape of 2026 is full of fun new denim cuts, some new and some which I’ve definitely seen and worn before. To help me figure out how to best style them without feeling like without feeling like a teenager or an influencer, I tapped the knowledge of four well-known stylists. I relied on them to point me in the right direction for cut, fit and comfort, and to help me properly style my new looks with tops, jackets and shoes.
As executive stylist and creative director Karima El-Hakkaoui says, “Ultimately, I want my jeans to work hard in my wardrobe. The more ways I can style them, the better.”

articles.title: My childhood was one of survival and resilience. How can I model a joyful life for my kids? | Leading questions
articles.summary: Start with the feeling, not the activities, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Making more room for enjoyment is also making more room for your actual self. I’m a child of first-generation immigrants and have always carried a story of survival and resilience.
body: I want to say it’s because my upbringing was not full of leisure activities; my parents only allowed us to focus on academic topics. Now that I’m a mother though, I wonder how I can role model some of this “living well for its own sake” for my children. It’s hard to find simple joys actually joyful. Growing up, everything needed to be “applied” towards something, and it feels that mentality is informing everything I do. Any advice on how to break free and live in the moment?

Eleanor says: Sometimes the means take over the end. Like a strangler fig. We start out doing something as a way of achieving something else we value – as a means to an end. But over time, it takes up so much of our schedule and mental prioritisation that it starts to twist and wrap around the things we actually value. It crowds them out, competes for vital nutrients, until it wins. It becomes the thing we value for its own sake; the means become the end.
It happens with money. We start trying to get money for the good life it’ll bring, but over time we’ll throw parts of a good life on a pyre for the sake of getting more money.

Making more room for enjoyment is also making more room for your actual self.

articles.title: Inside Gabby Thomas and Spencer McManes’s Romantic Rainy-Day Wedding in Cabo
articles.summary: It rained nearly the entire day when the three-time Olympic gold medalist married the beverage brand founder in Mexico—but just as she reached the altar, the skies cleared and a rainbow appeared over the Pacific Ocean.
body: It all started with an Instagram follow. Track and field Olympian Gabby Thomas and Kaviva non-alcoholic beverage brand founder Spencer McManes had mutual friends, but it wasn’t until Gabby followed Spencer back that he made his move. “He slid into my DMs almost instantaneously,” the sprinter and three-time Olympic gold medalist remembers. What began as a direct message soon led to a first date at a speakeasy in downtown Austin, where the two spent three hours talking about everything from pizza to Game of Thrones.
“Looking back, it’s wild to think our story started with a phone notification that could’ve just been a fleeting message,” Gabby says.

Spencer proposed nearly two and a half years later, in March 2025, on an Austin rooftop overlooking the city. “I had planned a staycation for us to celebrate the start of her season, as I had done the previous two years,” Spencer explains. “Gabby’s friends were a huge help getting the flowers and candles set up on the rooftop, and then they hid as I walked her up.”

articles.title: How Palace Kept Its Cool
articles.summary: Balancing subcultural capital with global growth and blue-chip collaborations is no mean feat. For Palace co-founder Gareth Skewis, physical retail and integrity go a long way.
body: It’s rare that almost every member of a company’s upper management team is a diehard skateboarder. But at Palace — the British apparel brand founded in 2009 — it’s par for the course. Gareth Skewis, who co-founded the company with Lev Tanju, cites this as one of the core reasons the international, multi-million-pound business has been able to expand and maintain its credibility in subcultures across the globe.

This week, the brand aired an exclusive capsule with Burberry at its new store on London’s Poland Street — a milestone for a brand that bet on quintessentially British skate style at a time when competitors were largely inspired by North American streetwear. Burberry and Palace had many conversations over the years, discussing projects and the right time to make the collaboration happen, Skewis tells Vogue Business. Then, the right opportunity arrived. “They’ve been amazing. [Burberry creative director] Daniel Lee and his team, and [CEO] Joshua Schulman have been really great to work with.”

For Palace co-founder Gareth Skewis, physical retail and integrity go a long way.

articles.title: Exclusive: The Making of the Costumes of ‘Dune: Part Three’
articles.summary: In an exclusive first look, costume designer Jacqueline West reveals how she drew on everything from medieval religious dress and Howard Hughes to Cristóbal Balenciaga for the desert epic.
body: Somewhere between the paintings of Giotto, the papal courts of medieval Europe, and a mesmerizing photograph of a wealthy woman wearing Dior sunglasses in Iran, Jacqueline West found the visual language for Dune: Part Three. There was Howard Hughes, too, the eccentric American billionaire who spent years living in near-total seclusion in a Las Vegas hotel penthouse, whose lonely existence became a reference for Timothée Chalamet’s burdened Emperor Paul Atreides. And then came Carrie, the 1976 horror film starring Sissy Spacek, which inspired Anya Taylor-Joy’s costumes. For a film set thousands of years in the future, West found herself looking further into the sands of time than ever.

articles.title: Ask a Local: Where to Go in Nairobi According to Runner Emily Chepkor
articles.summary: From scenic running routes to vintage shopping in flea markets, the founder of We Run Nairobi shows you how to fall for the city on foot.
body: " Nairobi is a city best understood in motion," says Emily Chepkor, founder of We Run Nairobi, the city's biggest and most popular run club. She's from a small town in Kenya, Kapsabet, that has produced more world-class runners per square mile than anywhere else on earth. While the country is known worldwide for its running heritage, Nairobi hadn't quite caught up to the hype until Chepkor came along.

She runs as a hobby, and is a 12-time marathoner (and two-time Boston qualifier) who felt that, though Kenya's running reputation was unmatched internationally, the runner lifestyle itself wasn't accessible to everyday Kenyans—elite athletes only. She set out to change that and bring running closer to all Nairobians, starting with a weekly run club that began with just her and three friends. It slowly grew through word of mouth and especially TikTok, into something bigger, built on a simple idea: no registration, no fees, you just show up and run alongside Emily.
